what: A sweep of the FULL git history for secrets committed before the repository went public (2026-08-01), plus everything since. Publication does not trim history, so anything ever committed is public regardless of whether it is in the current tree.
method: Scanned every BLOB reachable from every ref (`git cat-file --batch-all-objects`), not only the commits on master and not only the current tree — a deleted file's blob survives. Then a per-path pass across all 661 revisions to map any match back to the file that carried it.

credential_shapes.verdict: ALL BENIGN — every match lives in the repo's own SECRET SCRUBBER and its fixtures.
credential_shapes.why_that_is_not_a_leak: This is the code that DETECTS secrets, so it necessarily contains their shapes. The fixtures are synthetic: the AWS values begin `AKIAIOSF…`, the prefix of AWS's own documented example key. The per-revision pass confirmed these five paths are the ONLY ones that have EVER carried such a pattern in 661 revisions — there is no .env, no config file, no accidental paste anywhere else in history.

shapeless_pass.emails: 0 real addresses in blob content (excluding .invalid / example. / noreply / test fixtures).
shapeless_pass.private_ips: 0. The three initial matches (10.2.0, 10.6.0, 10.9.2) were VERSION NUMBERS caught by a loose regex — npm 10.9.2 appears in this repo's own artifacts. Recorded because the false positive is instructive.
shapeless_pass.env_files: No file matching .env has EVER been tracked.

verdict: CLEAN. No credential, key, token, private address or .env file has been committed in this repository's history.
honest_limits: This searched SHAPES. A bare password, an unmarked internal URL, or a credential with no recognisable prefix would not match any pattern here and would not be caught.
Git AUTHOR metadata carries the owner's email on every commit. That is inherent to git and to any public repository; it is not a finding, but it is a fact of publication.
Scope is this repository's object database. It says nothing about anything pushed elsewhere.
instrument_failures_caught_during_this_s: A `sed` with an invalid repetition count aborted the pipeline, making 63 real matches print as NOTHING. Trusting that run would have reported the history as clean on the strength of a broken command.
A grep pattern beginning with `-----BEGIN` was parsed as command-line OPTIONS and errored out; the private-key class was silently unsearched until re-run with `-e`.
Both are the same class: output that passed through a failing command is not evidence. Counts, not silence, are what make a negative result trustworthy — which is why every count above is stated.
